group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man presented to the pre-operative medicine clinic eight days before a scheduled open repair of a 6.2-cm descending thoracic aortic aneurysm that had been discovered incidentally on surveillance CT performed for chronic back discomfort; the cardiothoracic surgery team anticipates a left posterolateral thoracotomy extending from the fourth to the ninth interspace, temporary single-lung ventilation, use of partial left heart bypass with femoral cannulation, an operative duration of five to six hours, anticipated blood loss of 800–1200 mL, and immediate postoperative admission to the cardiothoracic intensive-care unit for neuromonitoring, spinal cord protection measures, and ventilatory support. The patient drove himself from a rural town two hours away, walked briskly from the parking structure to the clinic on the second floor without pausing, and chatted comfortably throughout registration, stating that at home he mows a half-acre lawn with a self-propelled push mower in forty-minute sessions, splits firewood for ten-minute stretches, and routinely climbs twelve basement stairs carrying laundry baskets without needing to catch his breath. He denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower-extremity swelling, or prior inpatient treatment for fluid overload; he sleeps flat on a single pillow and last weighed himself this morning noting no abrupt change. He has never been diagnosed with congestive heart failure and has had no hospitalizations for decompensated cardiac function. Medical history is significant for sixteen years of type 2 diabetes mellitus, initially managed with metformin but transitioned to injectable therapy four years ago as fasting glucose values crept above 200 mg/dL despite lifestyle changes. He now administers insulin glargine 26 units subcutaneously at bedtime and employs insulin lispro using a 1:12 carbohydrate ratio with a correction dose of one unit for every 30 mg/dL above 140; glucometer logs brought to clinic show pre-breakfast readings ranging from 108 to 156 mg/dL with no values under 70 mg/dL in the past month. Long-standing essential hypertension is treated with amlodipine 5 mg each morning and losartan 100 mg nightly, yielding home readings that average 124/72 mm Hg. Hyperlipidemia is addressed with atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and he chews nicotine gum after quitting a 30-pack-year smoking habit six years earlier; he consumes two beers on Saturday evenings and denies recreational drug use. There is no personal history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid endarterectomy, or focal neurologic deficits. Prior operations include an uncomplicated laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair at age 35 and arthroscopic meniscectomy of the right knee at 42. His father succumbed to complications of an abdominal aortic aneurysm at 67, and his older sister has insulin-requiring diabetes; no first-degree relatives experienced early-onset neurologic events. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, cough, exertional dizziness, claudication, abdominal pain, melena, urinary changes, or unintended weight loss. After five minutes seated quietly, vital signs recorded in the right arm showed blood pressure 128/70 mm Hg, regular pulse 68 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air, oral temperature 36.7 °C, height 178 cm, weight 94 kg, body mass index 29.6 kg/m². He appeared well nourished, comfortable, and euvolemic. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated, carotid impulses were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was localized in the fifth interspace at the mid-clavicular line without displacement. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp first and second heart sound with no gallop or murmur. Lungs were clear to percussion and auscultation bilaterally, with full expansion and no wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi. Abdominal examination demonstrated soft, non-tender viscera, no pulsatile masses, and active bowel sounds; there was an old periumbilical trocar scar. Extremities were warm with 2+ radial, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses, no edema, clubbing, or cyanosis. Neurologic screening revealed full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 motor strength, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, rapid alternating movements intact, and a steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour before the visit yielded hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, white blood cell count 7.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.34 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 58 mL/min/1.73 m²; simultaneous fasting glucose was 132 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today displayed normal sinus rhythm at 66 beats/min, PR interval 158 ms, QRS duration 94 ms, axis 40°, and no significant ST-T wave abnormalities compared with a tracing from last year. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography revealed a prominent descending thoracic aorta consistent with the known aneurysm, normal cardiac silhouette, clear lung fields, and no pleural effusion. Airway assessment documented a Mallampati class II oropharyngeal view, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 6.5 cm, and full cervical extension without limitation. The anesthetic plan includes double-lumen endotracheal intubation for lung isolation, arterial line and central venous catheter placement, maintenance of mild permissive hypothermia for spinal cord protection, continuation of antihypertensive and lipid-lowering agents on the morning of surgery, reduction of basal insulin to 75 % the night before, withholding prandial insulin while nil per os with hourly point-of-care glucose measurements, and goal-directed fluid therapy guided by esophageal Doppler to avoid both hypovolemia and pulmonary congestion. Sequential compression devices will be applied in the operating suite, and subcutaneous unfractionated heparin will begin the evening of postoperative day 0. The patient demonstrated accurate teach-back regarding medication timing, bowel preparation, fasting instructions, and early postoperative incentive-spirometry use, voiced understanding of potential complications including bleeding, spinal cord ischemia, respiratory failure, renal dysfunction, and prolonged mechanical ventilation, and affirmed his intention to proceed with definitive aneurysm repair.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery: open descending thoracic aortic repair qualifies as both intrathoracic and suprainguinal vascular surgery, but this is one criterion → 1.
- History of ischemic heart disease: none documented → 0.
- History of congestive heart failure: none → 0.
- History of cerebrovascular disease: no stroke or TIA → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: uses basal glargine and prandial lispro → 1.
- Preoperative creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: creatinine is 1.34 mg/dL, below the cutoff → 0.
Total = 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
